title: Your sitting
hookLine: how long, where, with what object
tomorrow: dinner at Ava's. her grandma says grace, then looks at Mai. now what?

lines: TWO BEDS, TWO DESKS, ONE WINDOW.
cards: Mai just got the floor plan for her summer dorm: two beds, two desks, one window, and a roommate named Jess she's never met. No altar. No quiet corner.
No cushion. The photos of perfect meditation rooms online don't look like this. So where does she sit?
The suttas answer in one plain line, and it's roomier than any photo.

teach.h: A TREE ROOT, AN EMPTY HUT.
teach.b: Where: the Buddha's teaching on mindfulness of breathing, in the Majjhima Nikaya, begins with someone gone to the forest, or the root of a tree, or an empty hut, who sits down. No special room, no one's furniture.
Just somewhere quiet enough. How: legs folded crosswise, body held upright, mindfulness set up in front.

teach.h: UPRIGHT: THE POSTURE IS THE SEAT.
teach.b: The posture is the seat; the place is wherever you set it down. The edge of a bed works. A folded blanket on the floor works.
For a monk, an empty hut. For a student, maybe the half hour before a roommate wakes. How long: there's a story for that.
Sona, a monk, practiced so hard that his feet bled, and he thought about giving up.
The Buddha asked him: when you played the lute, and the strings were too tight, did it play well? No. Too loose?
No. Tuned, neither too tight nor too loose? Yes.
Practice is the same, he said. So the length of a daily sitting is a tuning question, not a contest: long enough to settle, short enough to come back tomorrow.
And the object: the breath, the one that teaching starts with. It needs no gear, and it travels.
Your seat isn't a room. It's a posture, a place you return to, and a length tuned like a string.

how: A Buddhist who sits daily may keep one place for it, a cushion, bench or chair at home; they sit upright, choose a length they can keep, and often begin with the breath.

o: a daily sit with a set place, posture and length
a sit you do only when a full hour is free
a cushion you buy and keep in a special room

games.q: where, how, how long — tap the pairs.
p: a tree root, an empty hut
pushed so hard he nearly quit
neither too tight nor too loose

s: you need a cushion and a quiet room to meditate properly
the sutta's seat is a forest, a tree root, an empty hut: anywhere you can sit upright.
the Buddha compared practice to tuning a lute
not too tight, not too loose: his advice to Sona.
the longer you sit each day, the better your practice
Sona strained so hard he nearly quit; the Buddha told him to tune the effort, not max it out.

games.q: your friend sits forty minutes every day, but lately she dreads it and keeps skipping. what would the Buddha's advice to Sona suggest?
o: tune it: a shorter, steady sit she can keep, neither strained nor slack
push through: forty minutes a day or it doesn't really count
drop the daily sit until she feels like sitting again
games.why: the lute plays only when its strings are neither too tight nor too loose. a daily sitting is tuned the same way.

practice: Set your seat right where you are: sit upright, hands resting, back free of the chair if you can. Close your eyes and tune the effort like Sona's string, not tight, not slack.
Let the breath be the one thing you hold for two minutes.

wordCard.voice: Your sitting: a posture, a place you come back to, and a length tuned like a lute string.

orig.note: Pali: sitting cross-legged. In the suttas the meditator folds the legs crosswise before setting up mindfulness.

carryVoice: Carry this: your seat, which travels with you wherever you set it down. The rest is just furniture.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 118 (Anapanasati Sutta): the setting and posture
Anguttara Nikaya 6.55 (Sona): the simile of the lute
